opus-5.5.text:
So historically, if you look at the decomposition of AI progress, a large share has come from scaling up compute. Training compute for frontier models has been growing at something like four to five times per year, and that's been the main driver. Algorithmic progress, meaning better architectures, training methods and data, has also mattered a lot. Our estimates suggest the compute needed to reach a given level of performance falls by roughly half every eight months or so, which is substantial but still somewhat secondary to raw compute scaling.

The reason I think software could become dominant has to do with what happens once AI systems can meaningfully contribute to AI research itself. Compute scaling has physical bottlenecks. You need fabs, energy, data centers, capital, and those take years to build out. There are real limits on how fast you can pour concrete and bring new power online. Software improvements don't face those constraints in the same way. If you have AI systems that can do the work of research engineers, like running experiments, writing code, coming up with ideas and debugging training runs, then you can potentially run very many copies of them in parallel on your existing hardware.

That creates a possible feedback loop: better AI leads to faster algorithmic progress, which leads to better AI, and so on, without having to wait for the hardware supply chain to catch up. That's the core of the software intelligence explosion argument.

That said, I'm somewhat cautious about how strong this effect will be. One key question is how much algorithmic progress really depends on compute for experimentation. A lot of software innovation has historically come from running many experiments at scale, so if experiment compute is a binding constraint, automating researchers alone won't produce an explosion; you'd be bottlenecked on compute again. Another question is whether ideas get harder to find. Returns to research effort may diminish fast enough to offset the extra researcher labor.

So my view is that software's share of progress is likely to grow as automation of research ramps up, and could dominate for a period. But how much acceleration we get depends on these complementarities between cognitive labor and compute, which are empirical questions we're still trying to pin down.

r001.rationale: It contrasts hardware buildout taking years with software improvements that do not face those same constraints.

r002.rationale: It says AI systems could perform AI research work, accelerating algorithmic progress and making software a larger contributor.

r003.rationale: It explains that if compute for experimentation is binding, automating researchers leaves progress bottlenecked on compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I'd frame it is that AI progress, at least over the past decade or so, has come from a few distinct sources. One is compute scaling, just throwing more hardware at training runs. Another is algorithmic progress, which is roughly how much more you can get out of a fixed amount of compute, through things like better architectures, better optimizers, better data curation, better training recipes. And when we've tried to decompose historical progress, we find these two have been contributing on roughly comparable scales. Compute has been growing something like four or five x per year, and algorithmic efficiency has been improving at a rate that's not far off from that, maybe a doubling every eight months or so in some domains.

Now the thing about compute is that it's bottlenecked on the physical world. You need fabs, you need chips, you need energy, you need capital. Those can grow quickly, but they're constrained by how fast you can build things and by how much money people are willing to spend. There are pretty hard limits on how long you can sustain a four or five x per year increase in training compute before you're spending a meaningful fraction of global GDP.

Algorithmic progress is different because its main input is cognitive labor. It's researchers and engineers running experiments, forming hypotheses, debugging, iterating. And that's precisely the kind of thing AI systems are becoming good at. So you get this potential feedback loop where AI systems start doing a substantial share of the research that improves AI systems. Once that happens, the input to algorithmic progress is no longer constrained by the number of human researchers. It's constrained by how much inference compute you want to allocate to automated researchers, and that can scale much more flexibly than building new fabs.

So my view is that when you get to a point where AI can substantively substitute for human researchers, the software side of the equation could accelerate quite dramatically, while the hardware side continues on something like its current trajectory. And in that world, software becomes the dominant driver, at least for a period. Whether that period is long or short depends on how quickly you hit diminishing returns in algorithms, which is genuinely uncertain, but I think the historical evidence suggests there's a lot of headroom still.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts flexible software progress with physically constrained hardware scaling and says software could accelerate dramatically, but it does not clearly state that software advances can occur on shorter timescales.

r002.rationale: It describes AI systems doing a substantial share of the research that improves AI systems as a potential feedback loop that could accelerate software progress.

r003.rationale: It says automated researchers would be limited by the inference compute allocated to them, but does not state that researcher growth is constrained by compute needed to validate proposed innovations.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic reason is that software improvements let you get more out of the hardware you already have. You can make progress by building bigger clusters and using more compute, but you can also find algorithms that achieve the same performance with much less compute. Those improvements can accumulate and apply across a large number of systems.

The particularly interesting possibility is that AI itself starts to automate that work. If AI systems become good at writing code, designing experiments, and doing machine learning research, then we could substantially increase the amount of effort going into improving algorithms. You wouldn’t necessarily have to wait for new chips to be manufactured or new data centers to be built to benefit from that research.

So you could get a feedback loop: better AI systems help us develop better software, which produces more capable AI systems, which can then contribute more to research. That’s not guaranteed—experiments still require compute, and research might get harder—but it’s a reason to think software could become a much larger contributor to progress than it is today.

r001.rationale: The response says software research could yield benefits without waiting for new chips or data centers to be built, conveying that software advances can arrive sooner than hardware scaling.

r002.rationale: It identifies AI systems doing code writing, experiment design, and machine learning research as a way to increase algorithmic improvement and make software a larger contributor to AI progress.

r003.rationale: It notes that experiments require compute, but does not state that compute available for validating innovations constrains how many human or AI researchers can be scaled.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that software improvements can make better use of all the hardware we already have. You can get more capable systems by spending more on compute, but you can also get them by finding more efficient ways to train models, improving the architectures, or improving the data. Those improvements can sometimes substitute for quite large increases in compute.

And as AI systems become more useful for doing AI research itself, you could see that process accelerate. You could have systems helping researchers write code, design experiments, and discover better training methods. Those improvements could then make the next generation of systems better at research, too.

Hardware can improve as well, but designing chips and building fabrication plants involves physical processes that take time. Software experiments can potentially happen much faster. So if we become able to automate a substantial fraction of AI research, I think there’s a plausible case that improvements in algorithms and software become the main driver of progress. That’s a possibility, though, rather than something I’d regard as inevitable.

r001.rationale: The response says chip design and fabrication take time, while software experiments can happen much faster.

r002.rationale: It describes AI systems helping researchers write code, design experiments, and discover better training methods as a way software progress could accelerate.

r003.rationale: It does not say that scaling human or AI researcher numbers is constrained by the compute needed to validate their innovations.
